p: Welcome to the very first lesson. Before we talk about famous wines, grape varieties or how to serve a bottle, we need to start where every wine starts: in the vineyard. In this lesson we look inside a grape and see what its skin and its pulp each bring to the wine. Then we follow the vine through its year, from the first flowers to the harvest. We see what changes as the grapes ripen. And finally we discover why the climate of a region shapes the grapes, and so the wine, so strongly.

Let's begin with a simple definition. Wine is fermented grape juice. The grapes are crushed to release their sweet juice, and that juice is then transformed by fermentation, which we will explore in the next lesson. So to understand wine, we first need to understand the grape. There are two main kinds: white grapes and black grapes. And here is the first surprise: if you cut one of each in half, the inside looks almost exactly the same. The real difference is on the outside.

That outside is the skin. Black grapes have deeply coloured skins, and those skins hold something else too: tannins. Tannins are the substances that make your mouth feel dry, a little like a strong cup of black tea left to brew too long. White grapes, once they are ripe, have skins with a golden colour, and no deep colour to give. So whenever you think of colour and tannin in a wine, think of the skin of a black grape.

Now the inside, the pulp. It is soft and fleshy, and it holds the juice. That juice is mostly water, sugar and acid. The sugar will later become alcohol, and the acid will give the wine its freshness. And remember this detail, because it comes back again and again: the pulp has the same colour whatever the colour of the skin. Black grape or white grape, the juice is pale. Hold on to that idea; it explains how rosé is made, and even how a white wine can come from black grapes.

Next, the life of the vine. Grapes are the fruit of the grape vine, a plant that can live for several decades. A young vine is not productive straight away: it needs a couple of years after planting to reach maturity. From then on, it gives a crop of grapes every single year. And that year follows the seasons in a very regular rhythm, which is easy to learn.

In spring, the vine flowers. The flowers are tiny and grow in clusters, and here is the lovely part: each individual flower becomes one grape. Just after flowering, the young grapes are small, hard and green, all of them, whether they will one day be white or black. Through the summer they ripen, and in late summer the grapes are picked. That moment is the harvest. So: flowering in spring, ripening in summer, picking at the end of summer.

What actually happens as grapes ripen? There are five changes, worth learning in a row. The grapes swell with water. Their sugar levels rise. Their acid levels fall. Their flavours become riper. And their colour changes: white grapes go from green to golden, and black grapes go from green to purple. Think of an apple picked too early, hard and sour, and then the same apple fully ripe, juicy and sweet. Grapes follow exactly the same path.

Now, where do vines grow? A vine needs the right amount of sunlight and heat to produce good quality fruit. If it is too cold or too hot, it simply cannot do the job. It also likes a winter cold enough to let it rest. That is why most of the world's vineyards sit in two bands around the globe, roughly between thirty and fifty degrees of latitude, one band north of the Equator and one band south of it, where the grapes find the right amount of sunlight, heat and water.

Within those bands, we can separate cool and warm climates. Cool climate regions are closer to the poles; Germany and northern France are good examples. Average temperatures are low, the sunlight can be weaker, and in some years the grapes struggle to ripen at all. In cool regions it is common to grow white grapes. Warm climate regions are closer to the Equator, such as parts of Australia and parts of California. Temperatures are high, the sunlight is more intense, and the grapes ripen reliably every year. There, black grapes are commonly grown.

Why does this matter so much? Because climate shapes the grape. The cooler it is, the lower the sugar and the higher the acidity. The warmer it is, the higher the sugar and the lower the acidity, and the flavours taste riper. Take Chardonnay as an example. From a cool region it smells of green apple and lemon; from a warm region the same grape gives peach and pineapple. And since sugar becomes alcohol, warm-climate wines also tend to be stronger and fuller.

Here is a tip to remember it all: picture a thermometer standing next to the grape. As the thermometer goes up, sugar goes up with it, acidity slides down, and the fruit moves from apple and lemon towards peach and pineapple. As the thermometer goes down, everything moves the other way: more freshness, less sugar, crisper fruit. Same grape, different thermometer, different wine.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, the skin of a black grape brings colour and tannin, while the pulp holds a juice of water, sugar and acid that is pale in every grape. Second, the vine flowers in spring, and over the summer the grapes swell, gain sugar, lose acid, ripen in flavour and change colour, before being picked in late summer. Third, cool climates give grapes with less sugar and more acidity, while warm climates give more sugar, less acidity and riper flavours.

In the last lesson we followed the grapes all the way to the harvest. Now we carry them into the winery. In this lesson we look first at the one step that turns juice into wine: alcoholic fermentation. Then we follow three simple recipes, one for white wine, one for red and one for rosé. All three give still wines, meaning wines without bubbles. Sparkling and fortified wines are made in other ways, and those methods belong to a later level; here we keep to the essentials.

Let's start with fermentation. The workers behind it are yeast: microscopic living organisms, far too small to see. Yeast eat sugar, and as they eat it they convert it into two things: alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is a gas. So the whole story fits in one line: sugar plus yeast gives alcohol plus carbon dioxide. Learn that line by heart, because it is the heart of every wine, and the exam likes to check that you know both of the things fermentation produces.

In most cases fermentation carries on until the yeast have eaten all of the sugar. The result is a dry wine, which is what most wines are. The alcohol stays in the newly made wine, while the carbon dioxide usually escapes into the air, a bit like the bubbles rising from a pan of water close to boiling. There are exceptions. Sometimes the fermentation stops before all the sugar is gone, which leaves a sweet wine; sometimes the gas is trapped, which gives a sparkling wine. We meet both in the chapter on types and styles.

How do we measure the alcohol? With a figure called alcohol by volume. A wine at ten percent alcohol by volume is a wine in which ten percent of the liquid is alcohol. And here is the link with the vineyard: the sugar that the grapes built up as they ripened is exactly what the yeast turn into alcohol. Riper, sweeter grapes give the yeast more to eat, so they usually give a stronger wine.

Now, our first recipe: white wine. It is usually made from white grapes. After picking, the grapes are crushed, which breaks them open and releases some of the juice. Next, the crushed grapes are pressed, squeezing out the rest of the juice and leaving the skins behind. This is the key idea for white wine: the juice is separated from the skins before fermentation begins. The skins never get the chance to give colour or tannin.

Then yeast are added to the juice and fermentation starts. It can take place in stainless steel tanks or in oak barrels. Once fermentation has finished, the wine is matured, again either in stainless steel or in oak. Steel keeps things neutral, so the fruit stays fresh and pure; oak can add flavours such as vanilla or smoke. Finally comes bottling. So the white wine sequence is: crushing, pressing, fermentation, maturation, bottling.

A small detail that often appears in quizzes: a white wine can also be made from black grapes. Remember the last lesson. The colour of a black grape is all in its skin, and its juice is colourless. So if black grapes are pressed gently before fermentation, the pale juice can be separated quickly from the skins and used to make a white wine. Champagne, for example, is often made partly from a black grape, yet the wine is pale.

Our second recipe: red wine. It must be made from black grapes. After picking, the grapes are crushed, and this time the juice is not separated. Juice and skins go into the fermentation vessel together. Yeast are added and fermentation starts. During fermentation the juice and skins are mixed thoroughly, so that colour and tannin are drawn out of the skins and into the wine. This contact with the skins is the whole secret of red wine.

Once the fermentation has finished, the new red wine is drained off the skins. But those skins are still soaked with wine, so they are pressed to release what remains. Notice the difference: for white wine, pressing comes before fermentation; for red wine, it comes after. Then the red wine is matured in stainless steel tanks or oak barrels, and bottled. The red sequence is: crushing, fermentation, draining, pressing, maturation, bottling.

Our third recipe: rosé. It is made from black grapes and begins just like red: the grapes are crushed, juice and skins go into the vessel together, and fermentation starts. But after only a few hours, the juice is drained off the skins. At that point it is just pink. Without the skins it cannot get any darker, and it finishes fermenting on its own. Rosé is then matured, very rarely in oak, and bottled. The sequence: crushing, fermentation, draining, maturation, bottling. There is no pressing of the skins at the end, because they were removed so early.

Here is a memory tip. Picture the skins of black grapes as a tea bag and the juice as a cup of hot water. For a white wine, the tea bag never goes into the cup. For a rosé, you dip it in for a short moment and take it out: the water turns just pink. For a red, you leave it in for the whole time, and you get deep colour and that drying grip of tannin.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, fermentation is yeast eating sugar and turning it into alcohol and carbon dioxide; when all the sugar is eaten the wine is dry. Second, white wine is pressed before fermentation, so the juice ferments without the skins, and red wine is fermented with the skins, then drained and pressed afterwards. Third, rosé starts like a red but the juice is drained off the skins after only a few hours, and it is rarely matured in oak.

So far we have seen how still, dry wines are made: white, red and rosé. But the world of wine is wider than that. In this lesson we sort wines into their three types: still, sparkling and fortified. Then we learn the words used to describe any wine's style: its colour, its structure, meaning sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body, and finally its aromas and flavours. This chapter carries a lot of weight in the exam, so take it slowly.

The first type is still wine, and it is by far the biggest family. It is what most people picture when someone says wine: no bubbles. Still wines range from eight to fifteen percent alcohol by volume, and most sit between eleven and a half and fourteen. Many are named after the region where they are made, such as Sancerre and Burgundy in France, Rioja in Spain and Chianti in Italy. Others carry the name of their grape variety instead, such as Pinot Grigio. Knowing which logic a label follows is already a big step.

The second type is sparkling wine: wine that is bubbly or fizzy. Remember that fermentation makes carbon dioxide. Here that gas is trapped in the wine, and when the bottle is opened it escapes as bubbles. The best-known example is Champagne from France; Cava from Spain and Prosecco from Italy are also famous, and sparkling wine is now made all over the world. The third type is fortified wine. These wines have had extra alcohol added, so they are stronger, from fifteen to twenty-two percent alcohol by volume. The two to know are Sherry from Spain and Port from Portugal.

Any of these three types can come in many styles, and a style starts with colour. Colour depends on the grape and on how the wine is made. White wines are usually made from white grapes, such as Chablis or a Riesling, although, as we saw, a white can also come from black grapes if the skins are removed before fermentation. Red wines must be made from black grapes, whose skins stay with the juice during fermentation; Rioja and Cabernet Sauvignon are examples. Rosé comes from black grapes with only a short contact with the skins; White Zinfandel is the classic example.

Next comes structure, five characteristics you will learn to feel in your mouth. The first is sweetness, which is simply the sugar left in the wine. Most wines are dry, with no sugar or very little: the yeast have turned all the sugar into alcohol. Chablis, Sauvignon Blanc, Côtes du Rhône, Chianti and Cabernet Sauvignon are all dry. Most wines with a medium level of sweetness are white or rosé. They are made in two ways: either the yeast are removed before all the sugar has become alcohol, or some unfermented grape juice is added to a dry wine. Some German Rieslings and White Zinfandel are good examples.

Sweet wines have so much sugar that they can feel thick, almost syrupy. There are two key ways to make them. In the first, the grapes are so rich in sugar that the yeast stop working before they have eaten it all; Sauternes and some German Rieslings are made this way. In the second, used for fortified wines, high-strength distilled alcohol is added during fermentation; it kills the yeast before they finish, and the sugar left behind makes the wine sweet. Port and some Sherries are sweet for this reason.

The second structural characteristic is acidity. It comes straight from the grape juice, and it is what makes a wine refreshing. It is easy to recognise because it makes your mouth water, just like biting into a lemon. Too much acidity tastes unpleasantly sharp; too little and the wine loses its refreshing character. Chablis, Chianti and wines made from Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon or Pinot Noir all have high acidity. And acidity is vital in sweet wines: it balances the sugar and stops the wine from being unpleasantly sweet.

The third is tannin, a characteristic of red wines that comes from the grape skins. How much a wine has depends on the grape variety and on how the wine is made. Tannin can taste a little bitter, but mostly it is something you feel rather than taste: it makes your mouth feel dry. Red Bordeaux and Chianti are high in tannin. Beaujolais and some Pinot Noir wines are low in tannin. So remember the pair: acidity makes your mouth water, tannin makes it dry.

The fourth is alcohol. Most still and sparkling wines sit between eleven and a half and fourteen percent alcohol by volume, but some reach fifteen and others go as low as eight. Châteauneuf-du-Pape from France is an example of a high-alcohol wine; White Zinfandel from California is an example of a low-alcohol one. The fifth is body, the overall feel of the wine in your mouth. Just ask yourself: how mouth-filling is it? Think of the difference between skimmed milk and whole milk. Pinot Grigio and Beaujolais are light-bodied, Sancerre and Côtes du Rhône medium-bodied, Californian Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauternes full-bodied.

Finally, aromas and flavours. Some come from the grapes themselves, others develop during winemaking and maturation. Putting them into words is hard at first, but it comes with practice, and three families make it easier: fruit, oak and other. Almost every wine smells of fruit. The kind of fruit depends on the grape variety, so Cabernet Sauvignon smells of blackcurrant, and on ripeness: cool-climate Chardonnay shows green apple and lemon, warm-climate Chardonnay shows peach and pineapple.

Oak appears when a wine has been fermented or matured, or both, in oak barrels; sometimes the label even says so. It brings flavours such as cedar, cloves, coconut, smoke and vanilla. Then there is the family called other, which is part of what makes wine so fascinating: grass, flowers, herbs, vegetables, earth, mushroom and leather. Keeping these three drawers separate in your mind stops you from mixing up, for example, a vanilla note from the barrel with the fruit of the grape.

So what is a style? It is the sum of all these characteristics: colour, structure, aromas and flavours. Compare two French whites, Chablis and Sauternes. Chablis is dry, high in acidity, light to medium-bodied, with green apple and lemon and no oak. Sauternes is sweet and full-bodied, with apricot, honey and vanilla from oak, held up by high acidity. Here is a tip: think of a style as an identity card for the wine, with a line for colour, five lines for structure and a line for aromas. Fill in every line, and you have described the wine.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, there are three types of wine: still, from eight to fifteen percent alcohol; sparkling, with trapped carbon dioxide; and fortified, with added alcohol, from fifteen to twenty-two percent. Second, structure has five parts: sweetness from sugar, acidity that makes the mouth water, tannin from red grape skins that dries the mouth, alcohol, and body, meaning how mouth-filling the wine is. Third, aromas and flavours fall into three families, fruit, oak and other, and a wine's style is the sum of colour, structure and aromas.

There are hundreds of grape varieties that can make wine, yet only a handful have built a reputation all over the world. The grape, or the blend of grapes, is one of the main things that decides a wine's style and quality. In this lesson we meet the four key white grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio and Riesling. For each one we look at its structure, its typical aromas, whether it usually sees oak, and the places and wines it is famous for.

First, Chardonnay, one of the most popular and widely planted grapes on earth. It makes dry wines, but in a whole range of styles, because it changes with the climate. In a cool climate, Chardonnay gives wines with high acidity, a light to medium body and aromas of green fruit and citrus: think apple and lemon. In a warm climate, the same grape gives medium acidity, a medium to full body and flavours of stone fruit and tropical fruit: peach, pineapple, even banana.

Chardonnay also takes well to oak, which adds notes of vanilla. It is the grape of the white wines of Burgundy, in France. These are medium-bodied, with high acidity, lemon and peach, and sometimes vanilla from oak. On a label you may see the region's French name, Bourgogne, or the name of a village, such as Mâcon, Meursault or Puligny-Montrachet. Chablis comes from the coolest part of Burgundy: high acidity, light to medium body, apple and lemon, and typically no oak at all.

Outside France, Australia and California are well known for Chardonnay. A warm Californian example might be full-bodied, with ripe tropical fruit and vanilla from oak. Chardonnay is also one of the grapes of Champagne, where it is often blended with Pinot Noir. And a practical note: a full-bodied, oaked Chardonnay is served only lightly chilled, at around ten to thirteen degrees, so its richer flavours can show.

Second, Sauvignon Blanc. It makes dry wines with a pronounced intensity of aromas and refreshingly high acidity, and a light to medium body. Lift a glass and it practically jumps out at you. The fruit ranges from green apple to citrus such as grapefruit, and on to tropical fruit such as passion fruit. Alongside the fruit come herbaceous notes: asparagus, green bell pepper and freshly cut grass. That mix of zesty fruit and green notes is its signature.

In the winery, the aim is to protect those aromas. Sauvignon Blanc is often fermented in stainless steel tanks and is usually not matured in oak, because the wood would cover the grape's character. Two popular wines to know are New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc, from regions such as Marlborough, with grapefruit, lemon and grass, and Sancerre, from France's Loire Valley. Sancerre labels usually name the place, not the grape, so it is up to you to know that Sancerre means Sauvignon Blanc.

Third, Pinot Grigio, a hugely popular grape. Its wines are typically dry, light-bodied, with medium to high acidity and simple flavours of pear and lemon. It is not about power or complexity; it is the fresh, easy white you might pour on a summer terrace. To keep that fruity freshness, Pinot Grigio is usually fermented in stainless steel and not matured in oak. It is mainly associated with Italy, in areas such as Veneto and Trentino, but it is grown in other countries too, and it is a classic example of a wine named after its grape.

Fourth, Riesling, the acrobat of the group. It makes wines that range from dry, through medium, to sweet, but one thing never changes: every Riesling has high acidity. That acidity balances any sweetness, so even a sweet Riesling tastes fresh rather than sticky. The aromas are pronounced and can run from floral and green apple to citrus such as lime and lemon, and on to stone fruit such as peach and apricot. The body is light to medium. Like Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Grigio, it is often fermented in stainless steel and not matured in oak.

Riesling is the classic grape of Germany, where it is made in every style from dry to sweet. Some German Rieslings, from the Mosel for example, are medium-sweet, balanced by high acidity, and low in alcohol, sometimes around nine percent. Alsace in France and Australia, by contrast, make Riesling in a dry style, often with lime, lemon and blossom. So be careful: the word Riesling alone does not tell you how sweet the wine is. The place, or the wine's description, gives you the clue.

Now let's look at the four side by side. Three of them, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio and Riesling, are usually fermented in stainless steel and kept away from oak, to protect their fruit. Chardonnay is the one that often meets oak. So if a white wine shows vanilla, Chardonnay is a very good first guess. On acidity, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling are always high; Pinot Grigio is medium to high; Chardonnay depends on the climate.

Here is a memory tip: give each grape a personality. Chardonnay is the chameleon, changing with climate and oak, from apple and lemon to peach, pineapple and vanilla. Sauvignon Blanc is the green one, with grapefruit, passion fruit, grass and asparagus. Pinot Grigio is the quiet one, light and simple, with pear and lemon. And Riesling is the acrobat, from dry to sweet but always on the tightrope of high acidity, with flowers, lime and peach.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Chardonnay changes with climate, apple and lemon when cool, peach and pineapple when warm, often takes oak and vanilla, and is the grape of white Burgundy and Chablis. Second, Sauvignon Blanc is aromatic, high in acidity, herbaceous and usually unoaked, famous in New Zealand and in Sancerre, while Pinot Grigio is light, simple and Italian in spirit, with pear and lemon. Third, Riesling can be dry, medium or sweet but always has high acidity, with Germany making every style and Alsace and Australia making it dry.

After the whites, it is time for the reds. In this lesson we meet the four key black grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, and one grape with two names, Syrah or Shiraz. Remember that red wine takes its colour and tannin from the skins of black grapes, so with these varieties tannin becomes a big part of the story. For each grape we look at structure, typical aromas, oak, blending partners, and the places where it shines.

First, Cabernet Sauvignon, planted widely around the world. It makes dry wines with high tannin and high acidity: you feel both the drying grip and the mouth-watering freshness at once. The body ranges from medium to full. Its signature aroma is blackcurrant, often with black cherry, plus herbaceous notes such as green bell pepper and mint. Many Cabernets are matured in oak, which adds cedar and vanilla. A full-bodied Cabernet from Napa Valley in California, for instance, might show intense blackcurrant and cedar.

Because its tannin is so high, Cabernet Sauvignon is often blended with other grapes. In Bordeaux it is blended with Merlot, which adds softness and body. In Australia it is sometimes blended with Shiraz, which adds spicy aromas. Cabernet is also grown widely in California, Australia, Chile and South Africa, where it often appears on the label under its own name. In Bordeaux, the label shows the place instead, so you need to know the grapes behind it.

Second, Merlot. Its wines are generally dry and medium to full-bodied, with medium acidity and medium tannin. That makes it softer and rounder than Cabernet Sauvignon. The fruit can range from red fruit, strawberry and red plum, to black fruit, blackberry and black plum. Merlot is often matured in oak, which brings vanilla. In places such as Chile and California it is used to make soft, fruity, easy-drinking wines: smooth, with plum and blackberry.

Merlot is Cabernet Sauvignon's classic partner, and the two complete each other. Merlot brings softness and body; Cabernet brings tannin and acidity. Bordeaux is the most famous region for this blend, and in some parts of Bordeaux, such as Saint-Émilion, Merlot is often the main grape. The Merlot and Cabernet blend is now made in many other places too. Think of them as a duo: one gives the backbone, the other gives the cushion.

Third, Pinot Noir, the most delicate of the four. Its wines tend to be dry and light to medium-bodied, with low to medium tannin and high acidity. The fruit is red: strawberry, red cherry and raspberry. Pinot Noir is often matured in oak, which can bring vanilla and smoke. If Cabernet is a deep, dark bass note, Pinot Noir is a lighter, brighter melody, fresh and elegant rather than powerful.

Pinot Noir is the grape of red Burgundy, in France; on labels you may see Bourgogne or the name of a village, such as Volnay. It is also the principal black grape of New Zealand, in regions such as Central Otago. When making red wine, Pinot Noir is not usually blended with other grapes. The big exception is Champagne, where Pinot Noir is often blended with Chardonnay, and the juice is kept away from the skins so the sparkling wine stays pale.

Fourth, Syrah, or Shiraz. It is the same grape: it is called Syrah in France and Shiraz in Australia. It makes dry wines that are medium to full-bodied, with medium to high tannin and medium acidity. The typical flavours are black fruit, blackberry and black cherry, together with spice: black pepper and liquorice. Many are matured in oak, which adds vanilla or coconut. Black fruit plus black pepper is the clue to spot it.

Climate shapes its style strongly. In the Northern Rhône, in France, Syrah can make medium-bodied wines with fresh blackberry and black pepper. In warm regions of Australia, such as the Barossa Valley, Shiraz becomes full-bodied, with jammy black cherry and liquorice, and it can reach high levels of alcohol, sometimes around fifteen percent. Same grape, two climates, two styles: fresher and peppery in France, riper and richer in warm Australia.

Now let's line the four up. On tannin, Pinot Noir is low to medium, Merlot medium, Syrah medium to high, Cabernet Sauvignon high. On acidity, Cabernet and Pinot Noir are high, Merlot and Syrah medium. On fruit, Pinot Noir is red, Merlot moves from red to black, Cabernet and Syrah are black. And on service: medium and full-bodied reds are served at room temperature, around fifteen to eighteen degrees, but never warmed by a radiator.

Here is a memory tip, a small fruit bowl. Blackcurrant with a sprig of mint: that is Cabernet Sauvignon. A soft, ripe plum: that is Merlot. A punnet of strawberries and raspberries: that is Pinot Noir. A blackberry dusted with black pepper: that is Syrah. When you taste a red, ask which corner of the fruit bowl it comes from, then check the tannin to confirm.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Cabernet Sauvignon is high in tannin and acidity, with blackcurrant, green bell pepper, mint and cedar from oak, and is blended with Merlot in Bordeaux, which adds softness and body. Second, Merlot is softer, with medium acidity and tannin and red to black plum fruit, while Pinot Noir is light, high in acidity and low in tannin, with strawberry and raspberry, the grape of red Burgundy and New Zealand. Third, Syrah in France and Shiraz in Australia are one grape, with blackberry and black pepper, medium in the Northern Rhône and full and jammy in warm Australia.

You now know the eight key grapes. But walk into a wine shop in Europe and you will often not see their names at all. In Europe, many wines are named after the region where they are made, and the label expects you to know which grape is inside. In this lesson we connect the grapes to six famous French wines: three whites, Sancerre, Chablis and white Burgundy; two reds, red Burgundy and Bordeaux; and one sparkling wine, Champagne. Learn these, and a wine list suddenly becomes much easier to read.

Let's start with Sancerre, from the Loire Valley in France. It is made from Sauvignon Blanc. Sancerre is a dry, medium-bodied white wine, typically unoaked, with high acidity. Its aromas are pronounced: green fruit such as apple, and herbaceous notes such as grass. So everything you learned about Sauvignon Blanc applies: a lively, aromatic, refreshing wine, kept away from oak to protect its fresh fruit and its green character.

Next, Chablis. It is made from Chardonnay, and it comes from the coolest part of Burgundy. Remember the thermometer from the first lesson: cool climate means less sugar and more acidity. So Chablis is a dry, light to medium-bodied white with high acidity and aromas of green apple and lemon. It is unoaked, so there is no vanilla, just crisp fruit and freshness. Chablis is the perfect example of cool-climate Chardonnay.

Sancerre and Chablis are easy to mix up: both are dry, French, high in acidity, unoaked and full of green apple. How do you tell them apart? Look at the extra notes. Sancerre, being Sauvignon Blanc, has more pronounced aromas and that herbaceous, grassy edge, and a medium body. Chablis, being cool Chardonnay, is more restrained, with apple and lemon, and its body can be lighter.

Now Burgundy, or Bourgogne in French, a region that makes both white and red wines. The French name often appears on labels of both colours, and some labels show the name of a village within the region instead, such as Mâcon, Meursault or Puligny-Montrachet for whites, or Volnay for reds. The rule to remember is wonderfully simple: in Burgundy, the whites are Chardonnay and the reds are Pinot Noir.

White Burgundy is dry and medium-bodied, with high acidity. It can be oaked or unoaked. Compared with Chablis, which comes from the coolest corner of the region, white Burgundy often shows riper fruit: still citrus such as lemon, but also stone fruit such as peach. When oak has been used, you may also find notes of vanilla. So think of white Burgundy as a step up in ripeness from Chablis, sometimes with a touch of oak.

Red Burgundy is made from Pinot Noir and is dry. It tends to have low to medium tannin, a light to medium body and high acidity. Its flavours are of red fruit, raspberry and red cherry, sometimes with vanilla and smoke from oak. It is an elegant, fresh red, the opposite of a powerful, tannic one. And that powerful, tannic red is exactly where we go next.

Bordeaux is a region in the south-west of France, and its wines are most often red. Red Bordeaux is typically a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Remember the duo: Cabernet brings tannin and acidity, Merlot brings softness and body. As in Burgundy, the label shows the region, or an area within it, not the grapes. Bordeaux also makes a famous sweet white, Sauternes, which we meet in the next lesson.

Red Bordeaux is dry and medium to full-bodied, with high acidity and high tannin. Its aromas are of black fruit, blackberry and blackcurrant, with cedar notes from oak. It is one of the classic examples of a high-tannin red: you clearly feel that drying sensation in your mouth. On a wine list, you might see names of areas within Bordeaux, such as Saint-Émilion, where the blend is often led by Merlot, or Margaux, where you would expect concentrated blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannin.

Finally, Champagne, the most famous sparkling wine in the world, from the Champagne region in France. It is made from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, often blended together. Yes, Pinot Noir is a black grape, but its juice is colourless, so if the skins are kept away from the juice, the wine stays pale. And the bubbles, as you know, come from carbon dioxide made by fermentation and kept trapped in the wine.

Champagne is typically dry, with high acidity, aromas of green fruit and citrus, apple and lemon, and notes of toasted bread. That toasty note is what sets it apart from simpler, fruitier sparkling wines. Champagne is served well chilled, at six to ten degrees, and the bottle is opened carefully, with a hand always on the cork, as we will see in the lesson on service.

Here is a memory tip that works wonders. Sancerre and Sauvignon both start with S. Chablis and Chardonnay both start with Ch. Burgundy is one region with two colours: white Chardonnay, red Pinot Noir. Bordeaux is the duo: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. And Champagne borrows one grape from each Burgundy colour: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Sancerre is dry, unoaked Sauvignon Blanc from the Loire with apple and grass, and Chablis is dry, unoaked Chardonnay from the coolest part of Burgundy with apple and lemon, both high in acidity. Second, in Burgundy, or Bourgogne, whites are Chardonnay with lemon, peach and sometimes oak, and reds are Pinot Noir, light, fresh and fruity with raspberry and red cherry, while red Bordeaux is a high-tannin blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot with blackcurrant and cedar. Third, Champagne is a dry sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with apple, lemon and toasted bread.

In this lesson we meet twelve more famous wines. They are not made from the eight key grapes, but you will find them on wine lists everywhere, so they are well worth knowing. For each one, keep four things in mind: the country, the type, meaning still, sparkling or fortified, the colour, and a few key style traits. We will travel in small groups: a sweet white and a rosé, three French reds, an Italian and a Spanish red, two sparkling wines, and finally two fortified wines.

We start in Bordeaux with Sauternes, a sweet white wine. It is full-bodied, with flavours of stone fruit such as apricot, honey, and vanilla from oak. Above all, it has high acidity, which balances all that sugar and stops it from tasting cloying. Sauternes is made from grapes so rich in sugar that the yeast stop before they have eaten it all. It is served well chilled, at six to eight degrees, among the coldest of all wines.

Next, White Zinfandel. Despite its name, it is not a white wine: it is a rosé, from California. It is unoaked, with a medium level of sweetness and fresh red fruit flavours of strawberry and raspberry. It is also the classic example of a low-alcohol wine, often around ten and a half percent. So whenever the exam asks for a low-alcohol wine, or a rosé with some sweetness, White Zinfandel should come to mind.

Now three French reds, and the easiest way to remember them is to line them up by body, from lightest to fullest: Beaujolais, then Côtes du Rhône, then Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Beaujolais is a dry, light-bodied red, unoaked, with fresh red fruit, raspberry and red cherry, and low tannin. It is the standard example of a light, low-tannin red, and because it is so light it is served lightly chilled, at around thirteen degrees.

Côtes du Rhône is a dry, medium-bodied red with red fruit, strawberry and red plum, and a spicy touch of white pepper. It can be oaked or unoaked. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, also from the Rhône, is the big one: dry, full-bodied and high in alcohol, often around fourteen and a half percent, with strawberry and cloves from oak. It is the go-to example of a high-alcohol wine.

Crossing into Italy, we find Chianti, from Tuscany; on a list you may see Chianti Classico. It is a dry, medium-bodied red with high tannin and high acidity, so it feels both drying and very fresh. Its flavours are of red fruit, red cherry and red plum, with dried herb notes and sometimes cloves from oak. Remember those dried herbs: they are part of what makes Chianti recognisable.

Then Spain, and Rioja. It is a dry red, medium to full-bodied, typically with red fruit, especially strawberry, and vanilla from oak. Strawberry and vanilla together are its signature; on a list you may see Rioja Crianza, described with exactly those notes. To tell Chianti and Rioja apart: both show red fruit, but Chianti is built on high tannin, high acidity and dried herbs, while Rioja is rounder and marked by vanilla. And of course, Chianti is Italian, Rioja Spanish.

Now the bubbles. Alongside Champagne, two sparkling wines are very well known. Prosecco, from Italy, is light-bodied, with green fruit such as pear and floral aromas; it can be dry or medium in sweetness. Cava, from Spain, is dry, with flavours of green fruit and citrus, apple and lemon. So Prosecco means pear and flowers, dry or medium; Cava means apple and lemon, dry; and Champagne adds that note of toasted bread.

Finally, the fortified wines. Remember that fortified wines have had alcohol added, so they range from fifteen to twenty-two percent. Sherry is a fortified white wine from Spain. It is made in a range of styles and can be dry, medium or sweet. So, as with Riesling, the name alone does not tell you how sweet the wine is: you need to know the style. If the alcohol is added before the yeast finish, the yeast die and the wine stays sweet.

Port is a fortified wine from Portugal. It is sweet and high in alcohol, often around twenty percent, and it too comes in a range of styles. Typically it is red and full-bodied, with high tannin and black fruit flavours such as blackberry. Port and Sherry are easy to keep apart: Port is Portuguese, usually red and always sweet; Sherry is Spanish, white and anywhere from dry to sweet.

Here is a memory tip: a quick tour around the table by country. France gives us Sauternes and the three reds, Beaujolais, Côtes du Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Italy gives a pair, Chianti and Prosecco. Spain gives a trio, Rioja, Cava and Sherry. Portugal gives Port, and California gives White Zinfandel. And watch the three classic traps: White Zinfandel is pink, not white; Sauternes is sweet, even though it comes from a region famous for dry reds; and Sherry can be bone dry.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Sauternes is a sweet, full-bodied white from Bordeaux with apricot, honey and high acidity, and White Zinfandel is a medium-sweet, low-alcohol rosé from California with strawberry. Second, the reds line up by body: Beaujolais light and low in tannin, Côtes du Rhône medium with white pepper, Châteauneuf-du-Pape full and high in alcohol; Chianti from Italy has high tannin, high acidity and dried herbs, and Rioja from Spain has strawberry and vanilla. Third, Prosecco is Italian, pear and flowers, dry or medium; Cava is Spanish and dry; Sherry is Spanish, white, dry to sweet; Port is Portuguese, sweet, red and tannic.

Wine is surrounded by traditions about how to keep it and how to serve it. Whatever their history, they should all have one goal: to put the wine in the glass in the best possible condition. In this lesson we see how to store wine, how to keep an opened bottle fresh, which temperature suits each style, how to open still and sparkling wines safely, which glasses to use, and what to check before you pour.

Let's start with storage. A wine stored badly first loses some of its character, and in the end it can develop real faults. Three rules prevent this. Rule one: for long-term storage, keep wine at a cool, constant temperature. Extremes of cold and heat, and big swings in temperature, can damage it. Rule two: keep wine away from strong sunshine and bright artificial light. Both the light and the heat it brings can make a wine lose its fruity character.

Rule three is about the closure. If a bottle is sealed with a cork, store it on its side. That way the cork stays in contact with the wine and stays moist. If the cork dries out, it can let air into the bottle, and air makes the wine lose its fruit. Bottles with a screwcap have no such problem, and can be stored standing up. So, in short: cool and steady, out of the light, and corks lying down.

What about a bottle you have already opened? As soon as wine meets the air, it slowly begins to go stale. The simplest help is to put the cork back in and keep the bottle in the fridge: it will stay fresher for longer. To go further, there are simple systems that keep the wine away from air. Vacuum systems use a small pump to remove the air from inside the bottle. Blanket systems pump a gas into the bottle that pushes the air out; the gas does no harm to the wine.

Now service temperatures. As a rule, white, rosé and sparkling wines are served chilled, while reds are served at room temperature or lightly chilled. These are recommendations, not laws: if someone prefers their wine at a different temperature, a good host respects that. Let's go from coldest to warmest. Sweet wines such as Sauternes are served well chilled, at six to eight degrees Celsius. Sparkling wines such as Champagne are also well chilled, at six to ten degrees.

Light and medium-bodied whites and rosés, such as Pinot Grigio, are served chilled, at seven to ten degrees. Full-bodied whites, such as an oaked Chardonnay, are served lightly chilled, at ten to thirteen degrees, so their richer flavours can show. Light-bodied reds, such as Beaujolais, are also served lightly chilled, at around thirteen degrees. And medium to full-bodied reds, such as Shiraz, are served at room temperature, fifteen to eighteen degrees.

Be careful with that phrase, room temperature. With air conditioning and central heating, rooms vary a lot, so the range of degrees is the better guide. If a red is too cold, never warm it next to a radiator: sudden heat can damage its flavours. Simply place it in the room where it will be served and let it warm up naturally. And to keep a white, rosé or sparkling wine cold until the bottle is finished, use an insulated container or an ice bucket. With a bucket, fill it with cold water as well as ice: ice alone works far less efficiently.

Next, opening the bottle. For a still wine with a cork, first remove the top of the capsule, using a capsule cutter or the small knife on a waiter's friend corkscrew, and clean the neck of the bottle with a cloth. Then centre the corkscrew in the middle of the cork, screw it in and draw the cork out gently. Once the cork is out, wipe round the inside and outside of the neck with the cloth.

Sparkling wine needs much more care, because the bottle is under a lot of pressure. Chilling reduces that pressure, but even when the wine is cold, the cork can fly out and injure someone. So here is the golden rule: from the moment you loosen the wire cage, the cork stays under your hand until it is safely out. Remove the foil and loosen the cage, keeping the cork covered. Hold the bottle at an angle, with the cork in one hand and the base in the other. Then turn the bottle, not the cork.

Hold the cork firmly so the pressure does not push it out too fast. Controlled like this, the gas escapes with a quiet little sigh, rather than a loud pop, and not a drop of wine is lost. That quiet sigh is the sign of a professional. A loud pop and a fountain of foam might look festive, but it wastes wine and can be dangerous.

Now the glasses. There are hundreds of designs, but the best ones share one feature: the bowl narrows towards the rim. This concentrates the aromas inside the glass, so you can appreciate them better. Typically, red wine glasses are slightly larger than white wine glasses, and sparkling wines are served in flutes. Glasses must be completely clean, because dirt or a trace of detergent can spoil a wine, and they should always be polished before use to remove any lingering dirt or finger marks.

Last, a quick check before you serve. Look at the wine: any haziness could mean it is faulty, and there should be no bits floating in it. Then smell it: it should not smell stale, nor of wet cardboard or vinegar. Here is a tip to remember the whole lesson: think of three enemies of wine, heat, light and air. Storage keeps out heat and light, the cork lying down and the vacuum pump keep out air, and the right temperature lets the wine show its best.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, store wine cool and steady, away from strong light, with corked bottles on their side, and keep opened wine in the fridge with the cork in, or protect it with a vacuum or blanket system. Second, sweet and sparkling wines are served well chilled, light and medium whites and rosés chilled, full whites and light reds lightly chilled, and medium to full reds at room temperature, fifteen to eighteen degrees. Third, when opening sparkling wine, keep a hand on the cork from the moment the cage is loosened and turn the bottle; then pour into clean, polished glasses that narrow at the rim.

Wine can be a marvellous partner at the table. Pairing food and wine is often presented as a complicated art, but at this level it comes down to two simple ideas: personal preference, and a handful of predictable reactions between food and wine. In this lesson we look at both. We meet the main features of food, sweetness, umami, salt, acidity, flavour intensity, fat and chilli heat, and we see what each one does to a wine.

Let's start with the most important idea: the person in front of you. When you recommend a wine to a customer or a friend, the first thing to consider is what that person likes and dislikes. You might find a particular pairing exceptional, but if the person asking for advice does not enjoy that style of wine, there is no point recommending it. Taste is personal, and good advice starts by listening.

The second idea is reassuring: for most people, most wines are an acceptable partner for most foods. There is no single correct wine for each dish. However, some features of food usually have a positive or a negative effect on wine. If you understand these interactions, you are never stuck recommending one particular wine with one particular dish; once you know what most people want to avoid, your options become almost limitless.

Before we look at the food, let's name what changes in the wine. The wine can seem more or less sweet, more or less acidic, more or less fruity, more or less bitter and drying, and the alcohol can seem more or less noticeable. Where does bitterness in wine come from? From two sources: the tannins of red wines, and oak. Keep that in mind, because tannic and oaky wines are the ones most affected by the troublemakers we meet next.

The first troublemaker is sweetness in food. A sweet dish makes a wine seem more drying and bitter, more acidic, and less sweet and fruity. Picture a dry, crisp white served with a sweet dessert: the wine suddenly tastes sour and thin, as if its fruit had vanished. The usual answer is to choose a wine at least as sweet as the dish, for example a sweet wine such as Sauternes with a fruit tart.

The second troublemaker is umami, the savoury taste found in foods such as mushrooms or ripe cheeses. Umami has exactly the same effects as sweetness: the wine seems more drying and bitter, more acidic, and less sweet and fruity. That is why a very tannic red, or a heavily oaked wine, can turn harsh and bitter beside an umami-rich dish. With such dishes, a fruitier wine with less tannin is usually a safer choice.

Now the friends. Salt in food is very wine-friendly. A salty dish makes a wine seem less drying and bitter, less acidic, and more fruity, with more body. So a salty snack can soften a firm red, and a wine that seemed a little lean on its own can feel rounder and more generous. Acidity in food is another friend. An acidic dish makes a wine seem less drying and bitter and less acidic, and sweeter and fruitier.

Think of a squeeze of lemon over grilled fish. That acidity in the food tames the acidity of the wine, so a very crisp white suddenly tastes softer and fruitier. But be careful the other way round: if the food is more acidic than the wine, a wine with low acidity can seem flat. A high-acid wine is usually the safest partner for an acidic dish.

Three special cases remain. The first is flavour intensity. A highly flavoured dish can overwhelm a wine, which then seems to disappear. A delicate, light white, such as a Pinot Grigio, would be lost beside a rich, spicy stew, so with intense dishes, choose a wine with enough flavour of its own. The second is fat and oil. Fatty or oily food makes a wine seem less acidic, which is why a fresh, high-acid wine can feel nicely balanced alongside a rich, oily dish.

The third special case is chilli heat. Chilli increases the burning sensation of the alcohol, so the alcohol in the wine seems more noticeable; and in turn, the alcohol makes the chilli feel hotter. A powerful, high-alcohol red with a fiery curry can feel like pouring fuel on a fire. With spicy food, a wine with lower alcohol is usually more comfortable, for instance a light, medium-sweet Riesling.

Here is a memory tip: picture a dinner party with two troublemakers, two friends and three special guests. The troublemakers are sweetness and umami: they make wine harder, more bitter and more acidic, and steal its sweetness and fruit. The friends are salt and acid: they make wine softer, smoother and fruitier. The special guests each have one trick: intense flavour drowns the wine, fat softens its acidity, and chilli turns up the alcohol.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, personal preference comes first, and for most people most wines go acceptably with most foods. Second, sweet and umami foods make wine seem more drying, bitter and acidic, and less sweet and fruity, while salty and acidic foods make it seem less drying, bitter and acidic, and fruitier; bitterness in wine comes from tannin or oak. Third, highly flavoured food can overwhelm a wine, fatty food makes it seem less acidic, and chilli heat makes the alcohol more noticeable, while alcohol makes the chilli hotter.

Drinking a glass of wine and tasting it are two different things. To get the most out of tasting, you need to take the same approach with every single wine. Do that, and you can write tasting notes that describe a wine accurately, notes you can come back to and compare later. In this final lesson we prepare for a tasting, and then walk through the three stages of the approach: appearance, nose and palate.

First, get ready. Make sure there are no distracting smells around you: no strong perfume, no cooking, no scented candles. Have a white surface, such as a sheet of paper or a white tablecloth, to help you judge the colour. Use a glass with a wide bowl that narrows towards the top; that shape concentrates the aromas and makes the nose easier to assess. And start with a clean palate, with no lingering flavours such as toothpaste or coffee. Ever tasted orange juice just after brushing your teeth? Then you know why.

Stage one is appearance, and at this level you look at just one thing: the colour. Tilt the glass over your white surface and decide: is the wine white, rosé or red? It sounds simple, and it is, but it already tells a story. A red wine has spent its whole fermentation with the skins of black grapes; a rosé only a few hours; a white has usually been pressed away from the skins before fermentation even started.

Stage two is the nose. Give the glass a gentle swirl to release the aromas, then bring it to your nose and breathe in. Ask yourself what the smells remind you of, and sort them into three families: fruit, oak and other. Fruit is almost always there. Its type depends on the grape variety and on ripeness: blackcurrant suggests Cabernet Sauvignon, while apple and lemon point to a cool climate, and peach and pineapple to a warm one.

Next, look for oak. If the wine was fermented or matured in oak barrels, you may find cedar, cloves, coconut, smoke or vanilla. Then the family called other: grass, flowers, herbs, vegetables, earth, mushroom or leather. Do not worry if words fail you at first; describing aromas is a skill that comes with practice. Every glass you smell adds a little more to your memory.

Stage three is the palate. Take a small sip and move the wine all around your mouth, so it touches everywhere. Here you assess the structure, the five characteristics we met earlier: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body. Then you note the flavours. Let's take the five one at a time, with a simple question for each.

Sweetness: is there any sugar? Most wines are dry; some have a medium level of sweetness, such as many White Zinfandels; and a few are truly sweet, like Sauternes, which can feel thick, almost syrupy. Acidity: does your mouth water? Pay attention to how much: the more your mouth waters, the higher the acidity. A Chablis or a Sauvignon Blanc will make it water a lot.

Tannin: does your mouth feel dry, especially on your gums and teeth? Tannin is mostly something you feel rather than taste, and you will meet it in red wines. A red Bordeaux leaves your mouth gripped and dry; a Beaujolais barely does. Alcohol: how warming does the wine feel? Most wines sit between eleven and a half and fourteen percent, but a Châteauneuf-du-Pape feels noticeably warmer than a light White Zinfandel.

Body: how mouth-filling is the wine? Imagine sipping water, then fruit juice, then a smoothie: each one fills your mouth a little more. A light-bodied wine, such as a Pinot Grigio, feels delicate; a full-bodied one, such as a Californian Cabernet Sauvignon, feels viscous and fills the mouth. Finally, the flavours: use the same three families as on the nose, fruit, oak and other. Often you will confirm what you smelled, and sometimes you will find something new.

Let's put it together with a quick example, in plain words. For a Chablis, the note might read: appearance, white. Nose, apple and lemon, no oak. Palate, dry, high acidity, no tannin, medium alcohol, light to medium body, with flavours of apple and lemon. For a Beaujolais: red; raspberry and red cherry; dry, high acidity, low tannin, light body. Short, clear and always in the same order.

Here is a tip: treat the three stages like a pilot's checklist before take-off. Look, smell, taste, always in that order, and never skip a line. A good way to practise is to taste wines in contrasting pairs: an unoaked Sauvignon Blanc beside an oaked Chardonnay, or a Pinot Noir beside a Cabernet Sauvignon. The differences jump out, and the vocabulary sticks.

One last word about alcohol and health. Enjoyed in moderation, alcohol is not regarded as harmful to health. But drinking too much can seriously affect behaviour, sometimes in dangerous ways; for some people alcohol can be highly addictive, and in excess it harms both short and long-term health. Many governments and public health bodies publish guidelines on low-risk drinking, and they vary from country to country, so check the ones where you live.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, prepare well: no distracting smells, a white surface, a glass with a wide bowl that narrows at the top, and a clean palate. Second, follow the same three stages every time: appearance, which is the colour, white, rosé or red; nose, with aromas of fruit, oak and other; and palate. Third, on the palate assess sweetness, acidity that makes your mouth water, tannin that dries it, alcohol and body, then the flavours, again sorted into fruit, oak and other.
